extractions.quote:
Introduction
High levels of autoantibodies directed against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) are associated with stiff-person syndrome (SPS). However, other neurological syndromes have been described in association with anti-GAD antibodies, defining a novel group of syndromes, collectively
named ‘‘hyperexcitability disorders’’. Here, we describe a
patient complaining for acute onset of involuntary jerk movements in his legs, associated with pathologically
increased level of anti-GAD antibodies.
Case report
A 62-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of progressive involuntary jerk movements in his legs with
unsteadiness during walking.

He also referred balance disorder for 2 years, without vestibular impairment, (as evaluated by the otolaryngologist), and a single episode of trunk stiffening lasted 1 month, about 6 years before, improved thanks to physiotherapy.
Clinical re-evaluation made 5 and 10 months after the second hospitalization, when the patient was still taking azathioprine, showed complete disappearance of the involuntary movements.
Further exams revealed high serum anti-GAD antibodies titer (10, 000 U/mL).

We excluded anti-GAD antibodies elevation linked to misdiagnosed insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; the autoantibodies typically found in diabetes mellitus type 1 were negative; furthermore, patient received oral hypoglycemic agents without worsening of disease for several years.
Although we could expect that the patient had type 1 diabetes (GAD is also a major autoantigen in insulin-dependent diabetes, and up to 35 % of SPS patients have coexistent type 1 diabetes [ 5]), for the aforementioned features we are more prone to consider this patient affected by type 2 diabetes.
The majority of patients with stiff-person syndrome present with oligoclonal IgG bands and an increased antiGAD-specific IgG index; in this case we found an isolated CSF elevation of anti-GAD antibodies titer, with normal blood–brain barrier permeability parameters, testifying anyway an intrathecal antibody production against GAD epitopes.

A 62-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of progressive involuntary jerk movements in his legs with unsteadiness during walking.
Neurologic examination revealed inconstant rhythmic spontaneous contraction of both gluteal muscles, conditioning gait instability; these movements were absent during sleeping, whereas they were exacerbated by voluntary or passive contraction of the same muscles, deep tendon reflexes evocation, tactile stimuli, emotional stress resembling startle reaction.
Cognition and cranial nerve examination were normal. Strength was preserved. Deep tendon reflexes were diffusely reduced, whereas patellar reflexes were brisk. Vibration sense was mildly decreased in lower limbs. Coordination tests were normal. Gait was broad based.

Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed myoclonic activity of the paravertebral, gluteus medius, and abductor muscles of the hip, lasting 50–60 ms and alternating with similar activity in thigh adductor group of muscles. ... Basal electroencephalogram recording was normal. Simultaneous encephalogram/electromyography recording and jerk-locked back-averaging analysis excluded the epileptic origin of the movements. Lumbar puncture showed CSF anti-GAD autoantibodies elevation ([1, 000 U/mL); cerebrospinal fluid glucose, total protein amount, cell count, cytologic examination were normal; oligoclonal bands were absent. Whole body CT scan excluded solid neoplasms.

The majority of patients with stiff-person syndrome present with oligoclonal IgG bands and an increased antiGAD-specific IgG index; in this case we found an isolated CSF elevation of anti-GAD antibodies titer, with normal blood–brain barrier permeability parameters, testifying anyway an intrathecal antibody production against GAD epitopes.

The setting of symptomatic therapy at admission could have masked the typical SPS electromyography finding of ‘‘continuous motor activity’’, although neurophysiological testing of the thigh muscles showed alternating myoclonic activity, that has already been described in patient with anti-GAD positivity.
